newsitem.title: USA: Exiles give cautious welcome to Castro/Pope visit.
newsitem.headline: Exiles give cautious welcome to Castro/Pope visit.

text.p: Cuban exiles gave a cautious welcome on Tuesday to Pope John Paul's acceptance of an invitation to visit Cuba but said the trip was more likely to benefit President Fidel Castro than the Cuban people.

"I believe a visit by a pope with the record of this one in his fight against communism and dictatorship will certainly be positive," Francisco Hernandez, chairman of the Cuban American National Foundation, told Reuters. "I am sure that the message he will bring will be a message of hope."

The pontiff accepted an invitation from Castro to visit next year during an historic meeting at the Vatican on Tuesday. Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said both sides understood there would be no limitations on what the pope could say or where he could go during what will be his first trip to the Caribbean island. No precise date was fixed.
While the pope is credited with a key role in the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe, Hernandez said he did not expect the visit to signal big changes for the people of Cuba.

"Castro is trying to change his image. He's been doing this for several years, changing his olive green suit for a dress suit. But I doubt the pope will be taken in by this," he said. "The reality is that nothing changes in Cuba."
News of the pope's planned visit was generally well received in Havana. Cuban television broadcast footage of Castro praising the pope and describing their meeting at the Vatican as a "miracle."

The Cuban American National Foundation is the leading right-wing organisation among the many exile groups in Miami. The huge Cuban community is united in its enmity to Castro but divided over how to deal with him. The extent of humanitarian, political and cultural ties gives rise to fierce arguments.
Most Cuban Americans are devout Roman Catholics but many have been dismayed by the pope's criticism of the 34-year-old trade embargo imposed on the island by the United States.

"I think it good that the pope goes to Cuba but I am worried about the position of the church. They are not clear on policy -- they criticise the embargo, Tomas Garcia Fuste, an outspoken commentator on the Spanish-language WCMQ whose anti-Castro tirades have an eager audience, told Reuters.

"This will good for Castro but not for the Cuban people," he said. "Everybody has been waiting for this but it is sad for me to see Castro go to Rome and get next to the pope when he's a criminal with a bad history with the Catholic Church."
Catholic schools were nationalised and priests expelled soon after Castro's revolutionary victory in 1959. Freedom of worship and religious instruction are still restricted.
Castro, who was educated by Jesuits, and the pontiff discussed the role of the Roman Catholic Church in Cuba at length during their meeting, the Vatican spokesman said.
Jose Miro, Bay of Pigs Veterans Association president, said he hoped Castro did not succeed in making political capital from the visit.

"Definitely I think this is a step towards democracy in Cuba," said Miro, whose organisation comprises former fighters in the disastrous U.S.-backed attempt to invade Cuba in 1963. "The visit is very favourable to the people so long as Castro does not manipulate them."

He said it would help Castro in his overtures towards Spain and Latin American countries, which take a less rigid line on Cuba than the United States. "He does nothing if it is not in his favour," he added.
